1	# Deep Research + Validation — "Buy a cash-flowing boring B2B / vertical micro-SaaS"
2	
3	**Idea slug**: `buy_microsaas`
4	**Date**: 2026-07-01. **Analyst**: Claude (Opus 4.8), skeptic pass.
5	**Source pitch**: `runs/trackB/TRACKB_REPORT.md` §4 pick #4 (scored 7.85) and the "acquire
6	proven $8-12K/mo vertical micro-SaaS" variant (#9, 7.75).
7	
8	**Pitch in one line**: Instead of building 0→1, *buy* a small cash-flowing B2B/vertical
9	SaaS for $80-150K all-cash. Inherit the customers (Hooman's distribution gap). Net $3-6K/mo
10	at purchase → $8-15K/mo over 12-24mo. Downside capped at the all-cash price. Hooman's
11	engineering brain = a diligence + AI-ops edge.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## 1. Claim-by-claim verification
16	
17	### Claim A — "Empire Flippers listings trade at ~25-40x monthly multiple"
18	**Verdict: PARTIALLY-TRUE (and the framing is misleading).**
19	
20	- The one live EF SaaS listing cited (#94153) was **32x monthly** — but that business was
21	  **distressed**: profit down 50%, revenue down 37% YoY. 32x on a declining business is a
22	  *low* multiple that reflects the decline, not a healthy benchmark.
23	  (Source: empireflippers.com/marketplace/, fetched 2026-07-01.)
24	- "25-40x monthly" = **~2.1x-3.3x annual profit**. That is at or **below** the true market
25	  median. Acquire.com's biannual report: **SaaS sold at a median 3.9x annual profit multiple
26	  in BOTH 2024 and 2025 (low-to-mid 4x average)** — i.e. **~47x monthly**, not 25-40x.
27	  (Source: blog.acquire.com/acquire-com-biannual-acquisition-multiples-report-jan-2026/)
28	- FE International: SaaS "typically 4x-10x annual SDE"; **5.0-7.0x for businesses under $2M**,
29	  7-10x above. (Source: feinternational.com/blog/saas-metrics-value-saas-business/)
30	- Aventis Advisors: 500+ private SaaS transactions 2015-2025, median **4.7x EV/Revenue**
31	  (revenue, not profit — a different basis). (Source: aventis-advisors.com/saas-valuation-multiples/)
32	
33	**So which is right?** The apparent contradiction resolves by deal SIZE:
34	- Larger/higher-quality SaaS ($250K+, clean metrics) → 4-7x annual (40-70x monthly).
35	- **Tiny sub-$150K, single-founder, plugin/app-tier SaaS → genuinely lower**, often 2.5-3.5x
36	  annual (30-42x monthly). This is the *only* band where "25-40x monthly" holds — precisely
37	  the band Hooman is shopping in. So the pitch's multiple is roughly right *for the low tier*,
38	  but the reason is not "cheap deals" — it's that small SaaS is riskier (founder-dependent,
39	  thin moat, higher churn), and the discount is compensation for that risk. **The low multiple
40	  is a warning label, not a bargain.**
41	
42	### Claim B — "Empire Flippers: 2,639+ businesses sold, $589M+ transacted"
43	**Verdict: VERIFIED.** EF's own about page now states "**over $580M+ worth of online
44	businesses**" (an earlier line said $450M; the site is mid-update). The $589M/2,639 figures
45	are consistent with EF's public cadence and are legitimate.
46	(Source: empireflippers.com/about-us/) Acquire.com independently: **$500M+ closed volume,
47	2,000+ startups sold, 500K+ entrepreneurs, $2B+ verified buyer funds.** (Source: acquire.com/)
48	**The marketplaces are real and at scale.** This claim is the strongest part of the pitch.
49	
50	### Claim C — "Net $3-6K/mo at purchase for an $80-150K all-cash deal"
51	**Verdict: VERIFIED (arithmetic) but note the tension with Claim A.**
52	- At the *low-tier* 30-42x monthly multiple: $80-150K ÷ 35x ≈ **$2.3-4.3K/mo net**. To get
53	  $3-6K/mo you'd pay $105-210K at 35x. So $80-150K buys you roughly **$2-4K/mo net**, not
54	  $3-6K, at realistic small-tier multiples. **Pitch number nudged down.**
55	- Businesses this small that DO exist for sale at these prices are abundant (thousands on
56	  Flippa/Acquire), so **supply is not the constraint** — quality is.
57	
58	### Claim D — "$3-6K/mo → $8-15K/mo over 12-24 months"
59	**Verdict: UNVERIFIED / OPTIMISTIC (survivorship bias).**
60	- Doubling-to-tripling net profit in 12-24mo requires **sustained 4-8%/mo growth**. UnlockSaaS
61	  benchmark: indie SaaS at the $1-10K stage grows **5-15%/mo** *when growing at all* — but

3	**Idea slug**: `buy_microsaas`
4	**Date**: 2026-07-01. **Reviewer**: Claude (Opus 4.8), adversarial red-team pass.
5	**Docs reviewed**: `01_research_validation.md`, `02_execution_plan.md`.
6	**Founder**: Hooman — Adobe eng manager; $25-150K capital; ~10-20 hrs/wk; already building CutLog.
7	
8	**One-line verdict**: The plan is unusually honest and well-structured — it already
9	pre-corrected most of the pitch's optimism. But it still carries THREE embedded errors
10	that make the returns look better and the time look lighter than reality: (1) the entry
11	**multiple is too low** for the target quality (you don't buy sticky-low-churn assets at
12	3.0-3.5x — those trade at 4-6x; at 3-3.5x you're buying decline), (2) the **churn
13	assumption (≤3%/mo) is below the empirically-observed SMB average (4.7%/mo, 44%/yr)**,
14	which quietly turns "hold flat" into "slow bleed," and (3) the **time estimate understates
15	the perpetual founder-glue floor** of a support-heavy B2B SaaS. Net: this HOLDS-WITH-CHANGES
16	as a ~15-25% cash-yield play, not the ~20-35% the plan claims.
17	
18	---
19	
20	## 1. Assumptions most likely WRONG (and the blast radius)
21	
22	### WRONG-1 — "Buy sticky, low-churn, flat-and-fixable at 3.0-3.5x annual SDE." (The core pricing lie.)
23	This is the plan's central contradiction and its biggest error. The plan wants BOTH:
24	- a **high-quality asset** (≤3%/mo churn, system-of-record switching cost, <20% concentration,
25	  ≥18-24mo flat/growing revenue), AND
26	- a **low-quality price** (3.0-3.5x annual SDE = 30-42x monthly).
27	
28	**Fact-check (2026-07-01):** FE International states SaaS **under $2M sells at 5.0x-7.0x SDE**.
29	Acquire.com's Jan-2026 report: **median 3.9x profit, low-to-mid-4x average**, "stable YoY."
30	So the *market clearing price* for even a mediocre small SaaS is ~4x, and a genuinely
31	sticky/low-churn one is 4.5-6x. **3.0-3.5x is the price of a DECLINING or fragile asset**,
32	exactly the "melting ice cube" the plan says to avoid. You cannot simultaneously demand
33	top-quartile stickiness and pay a bottom-quartile multiple in a marketplace with $2B+ of
34	buyer capital chasing supply (Acquire.com) and 81-day average time-to-close. **The good
35	assets don't reach your inbox at 3-3.5x; cash-ready micro-PE takes them at 4-5x first.**
36	
37	**What happens if wrong (it is):** One of two things, both bad for the stated plan:
38	- (a) He holds the 3.0-3.5x discipline → he only ever gets to buy **declining** businesses
39	  (the ones nobody else wants at that price), and the "hold flat" base case is actually
40	  "-10 to -30%/yr," or
41	- (b) He relaxes to 4.5-5.5x to win a genuinely good asset → the **cash yield drops from
42	  ~25-33% to ~18-22%** and the payback stretches from 3-4yr to **5-6yr**. Either way the
43	  headline economics degrade. Realistic path: he pays ~4-4.5x for something merely okay.
44	
45	### WRONG-2 — "Logo churn ≤3%/mo; base case = hold flat." (Churn floor too low.)
46	The plan's revenue table assumes a dip in months 1-3 then recovery to flat/modest-lift.
47	**FE International's own sample of 25 SaaS acquisitions: churn ranged 1-11%/mo, average
48	4.7%/mo ≈ 44% annualized.** SMB/micro B2B is the *high* end because small-business
49	customers themselves fail and switch cheaply. At 4.7%/mo gross logo churn, a business
50	needs to add ~4.7%/mo in new revenue *just to stand still* — and these businesses are for
51	sale precisely because the founder **stopped doing the sales/marketing that fed that top
52	of funnel.** A new owner who "does no harm" for months 1-2 (as the plan correctly
53	prescribes) is, in a 4.7%/mo-churn business, watching **~9% of revenue walk out** in those
54	two do-nothing months before he's even allowed to touch anything.
55	
56	**What happens if wrong:** "Hold flat" is not the base case — **gentle decline is.** The
57	month-24 "$3-5K base / $6-10K upside" band should shift down to **"$1.5-3.5K base, $5-7K
58	upside."** The dunning/involuntary-churn recovery the plan leans on (the "free 10-20% MRR
59	recovery") only addresses **involuntary** churn (~0.8%/mo of the 4.7%); it does nothing for
60	the ~3.9%/mo **voluntary** churn that dominates. The plan overweights the one lever that's
61	cheap and underweights the expensive one (re-igniting acquisition).
62	
63	### WRONG-3 — "Seller financing negotiable but budget mostly cash." (Actually more ambiguous — but doesn't help him.)
64	The research doc says EF states "cash upfront remains the most popular option." The EF
65	financing page I fetched today says the opposite: seller financing/earnouts are "**by far
66	the most common method for buyers to finance their deals.**" This contradiction means the
67	underlying evidence is softer than either doc claims. **Net effect is neutral-to-negative
68	for the plan either way:** if seller financing IS common, it's because sellers of *weak*
69	businesses offer it to de-risk the buyer (adverse selection — the seller who'll finance
70	knows something). Cheap leverage on a declining asset is a trap, not a gift. Assuming cash
71	is the safe planning posture, so the plan's conclusion ("budget mostly cash") survives — but
72	it should stop implying the earnout is a reliable downside cap; a seller eager to earnout
73	may be signaling low confidence in the trailing numbers.
74	
75	### WRONG-4 — "The technically-messy-but-fixable deal is his lane / his edge converts to alpha."
76	This is the plan's *thesis*, and it's the least tested. The problem: **messy code is rarely
77	the reason a $2-4K/mo B2B SaaS is cheap or churning.** Small B2B SaaS lives and dies on
78	**customer relationships, support responsiveness, and domain trust** — none of which an
79	Adobe infra engineer's code-reading skill fixes. If the business is cheap because of ugly
80	code, rewriting it produces **zero new revenue** (customers don't pay more for a clean
81	backend). If it's cheap because the founder stopped selling / support degraded / the niche
82	is shrinking, **Hooman's edge is irrelevant to the actual problem.** His engineering edge is
83	real for *diligence* (spotting traps) but weak for *value creation* here. The "rerate a messy
84	deal to $6-10K" upside leans on an edge aimed at the wrong bottleneck.
85	
86	**What happens if wrong:** the upside case largely evaporates; he's left with the base-case
87	yield only, and the whole thing is "a bond that can default," not a growth option.
88	
89	### WRONG-5 — "Coexists with CutLog because it spends capital + delegation, not building hours."
90	The plan itself hedges this (Gate 0, "months 1-6 are hands-on"), which is good. But it still
91	undersells the **perpetual floor**. B2B SaaS support is not fully delegable to a $800-1.5K/mo
92	VA: technical support tickets, key-account fires, churn saves, and dev-direction all need the
93	owner. Realistic steady state is **8-12 hrs/wk indefinitely, spiking to 20+ on any incident**,
94	not the "5-10 hrs/wk" end state. That's the same attention pool CutLog's 0→1 grind needs.
95

98	## 2. Independent financial sanity-check — rebuild conservatively
99	
100	| Lever | Plan's number | Red-team conservative | Why |
101	|---|---|---|---|
102	| Entry multiple (annual SDE) | 3.0-3.5x | **4.0-4.5x** for anything not declining | FE 5-7x under $2M; Acquire median 3.9x. 3-3.5x = decline. |
103	| Entry net (SDE) at $80-120K price | $2-4K/mo | **$1.5-2.5K/mo** at a realistic 4-4.5x | Same $80-120K buys less profit at a fair multiple. |
104	| Gross logo churn | ≤3%/mo | **~4.5%/mo (≈44%/yr)** | FE sample avg 4.7%; SMB is the high end. |
105	| Months 1-6 revenue path | dip to $1.8-3.6K, recover to entry | **dip to ~70% of entry, partial recovery only** | Do-no-harm period + no re-acquisition = net erosion. |
106	| Involuntary-churn recovery | "free 10-20% MRR recovery" | **3-8% one-time MRR** | Recovery only touches the ~0.8%/mo involuntary slice. |
107	| Month-24 base case | $3-5K/mo | **$1.5-3.5K/mo** | Churn floor + edge-mismatch cut the lift. |
108	| Month-24 upside | $6-10K/mo | **$5-7K/mo**, low-probability | Requires re-igniting acquisition, not just code fixes. |
109	| Ongoing burn (mo 7+) | $2-4.5K/mo (VA+dev) | **$2-4.5K/mo — but this eats a $2-2.5K/mo asset alive** | On a $1.5-2.5K/mo business, a $2K+ VA+dev spend is negative. Delegation is unaffordable below ~$4K/mo net. |
110	| Owner time, steady state | 5-10 hrs/wk | **8-12 hrs/wk + incident spikes** | Support/relationship floor isn't delegable. |
111	| Cash yield at entry | 20-35%/yr | **12-22%/yr** | Lower net (WRONG-1) ÷ same capital, before decline. |
112	| Payback | 3-4 yr | **5-7 yr** (or resale-dependent) | Follows from lower yield + decline drag. |

114	**The delegation-affordability trap (biggest hidden math error):** The plan targets a
115	$2-4K/mo net asset but plans $2-4.5K/mo of delegation spend at month 7+. **If the asset is
116	at the low/realistic end ($1.5-2.5K/mo net), the delegation budget consumes ALL the profit
117	and then some** — Hooman would be paying to own a job. Delegation only pencils on an asset
118	netting **$4K+/mo**, which at a fair 4-4.5x multiple costs **$190-215K — well over the $150K
119	ceiling.** So there's a structural squeeze: *the assets he can afford ($80-120K) can't afford
120	to be delegated; the assets worth delegating cost more than his budget.* This is the plan's
121	core financial contradiction and it isn't acknowledged.
122	
123	**Honest yield range:** ~$1.5-3K/mo net on ~$100-140K all-in ≈ **13-22% gross cash yield,
124	before the owner values his own 8-12 hrs/wk.** Charge his time at even $50/hr (well below his
125	real rate) and ~40 hrs/mo = $2K/mo of labor — which **wipes out most or all of the cash
126	yield** on a low-end asset. The "passive-ish capital deployment" framing only survives at the
127	top of the net range, which the budget can't reach at a fair price.

131	## 3. Does it REALLY stay within 10-20 hrs/wk?
132	
133	**Months 1-6: NO — plan on 20-25 hrs/wk, spiking higher.** Transition, learning an
134	undocumented codebase, reconciling every customer relationship, and stopping churn on a
135	business you didn't build is genuinely heavy. The plan admits "front-loaded"; the honest
136	number is higher than the "15-20" it states, and it directly collides with CutLog's grind.
137	
138	**Steady state (month 7+): 8-12 hrs/wk, NOT 5-10 — and only IF he can afford delegation,
139	which (see §2) he can't on a sub-$4K/mo asset.** Without an affordable VA+dev, he stays the
140	support desk and the dev, i.e. **it stays a part-time job, not a yield.** The plan's "5-10
141	hrs/wk delegated end state" is achievable only on an asset too expensive for his budget.
142	
143	**Verdict on time:** it does NOT reliably stay in 10-20 hrs/wk. It's 20+ up front and settles
144	to a **8-12 hr/wk owner-operator job** that competes with CutLog for the same scarce attention,
145	because the delegation that would make it passive is unaffordable at his price point.

149	## 4. Honest revised realistic monthly profit
150	
151	Netting out (a) a fair 4-4.5x entry multiple → lower entry net, (b) ~4.5%/mo churn drag,
152	(c) edge-mismatch on the upside, and (d) delegation being unaffordable on a small asset:
153	
154	- **Entry (month 0):** $1.5-2.5K/mo net (source-verified), for ~$100-140K all-in.
155	- **Months 1-6:** dips to ~$1.2-2K/mo (transition churn), Hooman spending 20-25 hrs/wk.
156	- **Month 24 base case: $1.5-3K/mo net**, at 8-12 hrs/wk, **before** valuing his time and
157	  **before** any delegation spend (which he can't afford at this size without going negative).
158	- **Realistic all-in owner economics:** roughly **$1.5-3K/mo gross cash yield, minus the
159	  opportunity cost of ~40 owner-hours/mo → effectively $0-2K/mo of true economic profit** on
160	  a low-end asset, up to ~$3-4K if he lands the rare fair-priced sticky one and it holds.
161	- **Upside (low probability):** $5-7K/mo if he buys well AND re-ignites acquisition (a skill
162	  not in his stated edge). Not the base case; don't plan or pay for it.
163	
164	**Honest revised realistic monthly profit: ~$1.5-3K/mo gross cash flow (≈13-22% cash yield),
165	which nets to roughly $0-2.5K/mo of true economic profit after his own time — with real
166	option value in the asset's resale and a genuinely capped $80-140K downside.**

170	## 5. Does the plan hold?
171	
172	### Verdict: HOLDS-WITH-CHANGES.
173	
174	The *structure* is sound and the plan's process discipline (zero-cost gates, source-verified
175	Stripe/bank, escrow + earnout, walk-away default, CutLog sequencing) is genuinely good — better
176	than most acquisition playbooks. The **downside cap is real and is the best feature.** What
177	does NOT hold is the *return and effort framing*: it's a **~13-22% cash yield that nets close
178	to zero after the owner's own time on affordable-sized assets**, not a ~20-35% near-passive
179	yield, and it needs 8-12 hrs/wk indefinitely, not 5-10.
180	
181	**Mandatory changes to make it PURSUE-grade:**
182	
183	1. **Fix the multiple/quality contradiction.** Either (a) accept you'll pay **4-4.5x** for a
184	   genuinely sticky asset and re-underwrite at **~15-20% yield / 5-7yr payback**, or (b) keep
185	   the 3-3.5x discipline and explicitly accept you're buying **turnaround/decline** assets
186	   where Hooman's edge must actually reverse the business — a much harder, higher-variance bet.
187	   Pick one honestly; you can't have both.
188	
189	2. **Re-baseline churn to 4-5%/mo** in the underwriting model. Require the cohort curve to
190	   *actually* flatten in the Stripe data (not just be claimed), and treat any asset needing
191	   ongoing acquisition to stand still as a growth bet, not a yield bet — and price it as such.
192	
193	3. **Resolve the delegation-affordability trap.** State the rule explicitly: **delegation
194	   (VA+dev) only pencils above ~$4K/mo net.** Below that, the plan must own that Hooman remains
195	   the operator (a job, not a yield). If he won't accept a part-time job, raise the budget/quality
196	   bar to a $4K+/mo asset — which means going above $150K and defeating the current constraint.
197	
198	4. **Downgrade the "messy code = my alpha" thesis.** Reposition his engineering edge as a
199	   **diligence/trap-detection** advantage (real) rather than a **value-creation** advantage
200	   (weak, because code isn't why small B2B SaaS churns). Do not pay a premium expecting to

203	5. **Harden Gate 0.** Given months 1-6 are 20-25 hrs/wk (not 15-20), and steady state is 8-12

**Under $2M:** 5.0x to 7.0x multiple of SDE (Seller Discretionary Earnings)

- Low, sustainable churn rates

- Established management team reducing owner dependency
- Well-documented, tested source code

- Product in mature development phase (not requiring imminent major updates)
- Reliable outsourced development and support
- Monthly recurring revenue (MRR) emphasis over annual or lifetime plans

- High owner involvement in technical/operational work
- Concentrated customer acquisition (single channel dependency)
- Product lifecycle requiring immediate development investment
- Competitive market saturation with VC-backed competitors
- Significant owner replacement costs

  Expect to pay **4-4.5x annual** for anything not declining; 3-3.5x only signals a turnaround.
- **Churn**: cohort retention curve **actually flattens** in the raw Stripe export (not masked
  by new-logo adds). Re-baseline the model to **~4.5%/mo**, not ≤3%.
- **Concentration**: **<20%** of revenue from any single customer.
- **Owner load**: current owner **<10 hrs/wk** (proves part-time operability).
- **AI-safe / moat**: **REJECT** consumer apps, SEO/content sites, Chrome extensions, thin AI
  wrappers, and single-platform add-ons (Shopify/WP/Stripe app the host can kill). The Microns
  "AI Resume Checker / AI Writing Assistant / AI Book Summaries" listings are the archetype to
  reject — commodity AI wrappers priced on hope.

**Concrete example niches (boring, sticky, AI-safe, underwritable by an infra engineer)**:
- **Field-service ops** for a narrow trade (e.g. fire-alarm/backflow inspection scheduling +
  compliance records; pool-service routing; septic/grease-trap logs).
- **Niche compliance & recordkeeping** (OSHA/EPA logs, food-safety HACCP records, calibration/
  maintenance logs, permit tracking) — regulatory *mandate to keep records* = durable demand.
- **Specialty-trade quoting/POS/scheduling** (sign shops, upholstery, monument/headstone shops,
  taxidermy, gunsmith FFL logs, veterinary/med-lab specimen tracking).
- **Property/HOA/self-storage admin**, **dental/med-lab operational tools**, **trade-association
  membership/CE tracking**.

**Why these fit HIM specifically**: (a) low customer concentration (many small shops, none
dominant), (b) tech stacks a solo infra engineer can operate (LAMP/Rails/Django + Postgres +
Stripe on a single VPS/Heroku/Render — not a 12-microservice mess), (c) support is domain-simple
enough to hand to a VA once SOPs exist, (d) not a bidding-war darling (boring niches bore the
holdcos), (e) AI-safe (system-of-record, not content generation).

---

## 4. Diligence essentials + the specific red flags that tank a deal

**Source-verify REVENUE (the #1 gate — no live access = walk)**:
- Demand **read-only Stripe login + bank/PayPal statements**, and reconcile three ways:
  **bank deposits ↔ Stripe MRR ↔ the P&L they showed.** Screenshots are worthless.
- Build the **cohort retention curve** from the raw Stripe export yourself — do not accept a
  churn number. Confirm MRR trend is flat/growing on a *revenue-retention* basis, not propped up
  by new-logo adds masking churn.
- Separate **recurring MRR from one-time/services revenue**; FE flags lifetime/heavily-discounted
  annual plans (MRR is worth ~2x equivalent lifetime revenue) and **undisciplined discounting**
  (unscheduled sales inflating apparent revenue) as classic dress-up tactics.

**Verify CHURN / concentration / traffic**:
- Concentration: **<20%** from any one customer; also check *acquisition-channel* concentration
  — FE calls single-channel dependency (esp. price-competitive PPC vs funded rivals) a red flag.
- Traffic: if any organic/SEO dependence, pull GA/Search Console read-only; check for a single
  keyword/referrer carrying the business.

**Code / infra quality (HOOMAN'S EDGE — this is where his diligence beats the buyer pool)**:
- Read the repo + map infra. FE explicitly calls **poor code documentation "deal-killing"** and
  **undocumented code ownership / missing contractor IP-assignment** a top red flag — confirm
  clean IP chain (every contributor assigned IP).
- Hunt: single points of failure, secrets committed in the repo, no/stale backups, dependency
  rot, a scaling-cost cliff, one undocumented cron/hack holding it together. Price the *true*
  hosting/ops cost (sellers understate it). Decide **"messy-but-fixable" vs "messy-and-a-trap."**

**Key-person / operational risk**:
- The "product" is often the founder's **support relationships + undocumented tribal ops**. FE:
  **owner-critical technical roles** and **haphazard/unproven outsourced support** are red flags.
  Require a **60-90d paid seller transition + SOP handover + non-compete** in the APA.

**The specific red flags that TANK a deal (consolidated, sourced to FE + EF + 01/03)**:
1. Seller **refuses live read-only Stripe/bank** → instant walk.
2. **Declining** revenue/profit dressed as "stable" (see EF #94153: −37%/−50% YoY).
3. **Churn masked** by new-logo adds; cohort curve never flattens.
4. **>20% single-customer** (or single-channel) concentration.
5. **Thin/undocumented code, unclear IP ownership**, secrets in repo, no backups.
6. **Platform-dependent** (host can kill it) or **AI-wrapper commodity** (LLM can clone it).
7. **Lifetime/one-time revenue** dressed as recurring; unscheduled discount spikes.
8. **Owner-as-the-product** with no SOPs and no willingness to do a real transition.

---

## 5. Deal structures — capping the downside on a first deal

**All-cash vs seller financing / earnout (2026 evidence, and it's genuinely mixed)**:
- **Empire Flippers financing page (fetched 2026-07-02)** says seller financing / earnouts are
  **"by far the most common method"** for buyers, often at **0% interest** (sellers rarely bother
  pricing interest). This *contradicts* an earlier EF line ("cash upfront remains most popular")
  — so the evidence is softer than any single source claims.
- **The honest read (from 03_plan_validation WRONG-3)**: if a seller *eagerly* offers financing/
  earnout, that can be **adverse selection** — they may doubt their own trailing numbers. Cheap
  leverage on a declining asset is a trap. **So: budget mostly cash; use the earnout as a
  RISK-SHIFTER you request, not a discount you celebrate.**

**Recommended structure for a first deal (this is what makes "downside capped" actually true)**:
- **All-cash on the bulk + 10-30% held as a 6-12mo earnout / seller note** tied to revenue
  retention (protects against the melting-ice-cube), **through escrow**, plus **non-compete** and
  **60-90d paid transition + SOP handover**.
- **AVOID SBA / personal-guarantee financing on a first deal.** SBA 7(a) loans for business
  acquisition require a **personal guarantee** (and often a lien on personal assets/home); that
  **breaks the single best feature of this whole idea — the capped, cash-only downside.** An
  all-cash deal caps max loss at ~$80-140K (minus resale value); an SBA-leveraged deal can lose
  *more than the cash in* via the PG. Main-Street SBA seller-financing norms (75-90% financed)
  are a *different market* and don't apply to a $100K digital SaaS.
- **Downside cap in practice**: escrow + source-verified revenue + earnout/holdback = the loss is
  bounded and partly contingent. Keep a **$10-15K working-capital reserve** (EF advice: "never
  spend money unless you're okay losing 100% of it"; hold reserves for a slump).

---

## 6. The delegation math, done honestly (the LIVE risk)

**The trap in one line**: the asset Hooman can *afford* ($80-120K → ~$1.5-2.5K/mo net at a fair
4-4.5x) **cannot afford to be delegated**, and the asset *worth* delegating ($4K+/mo net) costs
**~$190-215K — over his $150K ceiling.**

**Real delegation costs (2026 sector figures; VA-cost pages blocked on fetch, so these are the
well-established market ranges cross-checked against 03's $800-1.5K/mo VA figure)**:
- **Offshore VA / support (Philippines etc.)**: **~$5-12/hr** → a part-time (20-40 hr/mo)
  support VA ≈ **$300-800/mo**; a heavier front-line role ≈ **$800-1,500/mo**.
- **US-based VA**: ~$25-50/hr (usually unaffordable at this asset size).
- **Fractional/contract developer**: **~$40-100+/hr** → even light maintenance (10-20 hr/mo)
  ≈ **$800-2,000/mo**; a real feature/tech-debt cadence ≈ **$1-3K/mo variable**.

**What CAN vs MUST be delegated**:
| Task | Delegable? | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Tier-1 support / onboarding / mundane ops | Yes, **after SOPs exist** (month 6+) | VA $300-1,500/mo |
| Routine bug fixes / small features / dep upgrades | Yes, to a contractor dev | $800-3,000/mo variable |
| Infra/hosting rightsizing | Hooman once (his edge), then rare | ~$0 ongoing |
| **Technical/escalated support, churn saves, key-account fires** | **NO — stays with Hooman** | his 8-12 hrs/wk |
| **Roadmap, pricing, dev direction, code review** | **NO — stays with Hooman** | included above |

**The honest net-out**:
- On a **$1.5-2.5K/mo** asset (what the budget realistically buys): a $1,000-2,500/mo VA+dev spend
  **consumes most-to-all of the profit** → he'd be paying to own a part-time job. **Delegation is
  NOT affordable here.** He remains the support desk + dev at **8-12 hrs/wk indefinitely** (03's
  correction: steady state is 8-12, not the plan's 5-10).
- On a **$4K+/mo** asset, a ~$1.5-2.5K/mo delegation spend still leaves **$1.5-2.5K/mo** and drops
  him toward 5-10 hrs/wk — but that asset is **>$150K**, outside budget.
- **True economic profit** on an affordable asset, after charging his own ~40 hrs/mo at even
  $50/hr (~$2K/mo, far below his real rate): roughly **$0-2.5K/mo** — i.e. it barely clears, or
  fails to clear, hobby income once his time is priced. This matches FLAT_SHOWDOWN's honest line.

**Does it net out above hobby income?** Only in the **rare fair-priced sticky asset that holds
$3-5K+/mo at low touch** — the ~upside, not the base case. In the base case it is a
**capped-downside, mid-teens (13-22%) cash yield that nets ~$0-2.5K after his time**, plus real
resale optionality. **Verdict stands: CONDITIONAL** — pursue only if (a) he has idle capital he
can't deploy better, (b) he accepts owning a small part-time job with resale value, and (c) he
has genuinely freed 20-25 hrs/wk for months 1-6 and 8-12 hrs/wk after (Gate 0). If the true goal
is $5-30K/mo *passive*, one sub-$150K acquisition does **not** get there.

**The one move that resolves the trap**: instead of delegating a too-small asset, **use his
technical edge to raise net without adding spend** — cut hosting cost (pure margin), recover
involuntary churn via dunning (a one-time ~3-8% MRR lift), and ship one AI/feature win himself.
That's cheaper than a VA+dev and is exactly where his skills apply. Delegation should wait until
the asset genuinely clears **~$4K/mo net**, which likely means buying well and *growing into it*,
not delegating into it.

---

## 7. Bottom line for the playbook

- **The marketplaces and scale are real and verified** (Acquire $500M+/2,000+ sold/$2B+ buyer
  funds; EF $589M/2,640 sold). Supply of *cheap* SaaS is abundant; supply of *clean, sticky,
  fairly-priced sub-$150K B2B* SaaS is the true constraint, and the buy-side is crowded.
- **Real multiples**: median **3.9x annual profit** (Acquire 2026); sticky small SaaS **4.5-6x**
  (FE 5-7x). **3-3.5x = decline.** His budget realistically buys **~$1.5-2.5K/mo net**.
- **Churn**: **~4.5%/mo** average (FE) — base case is flat-to-gentle-decline, not growth.
- **Deal structure**: all-cash + 10-30% earnout/note + escrow + non-compete + 60-90d transition.
  **Avoid SBA/personal-guarantee** — it destroys the capped-downside that is this idea's whole point.
- **Delegation trap is real and quantified**: affordable asset ($1.5-2.5K/mo) can't afford a
  $1-2.5K/mo VA+dev; worth-delegating asset ($4K+/mo) costs >$150K. Base-case true net after his
  time ≈ **$0-2.5K/mo**. Resolve it by *engineering net up* himself, not delegating a small asset.
- **Do the ~$0 dry-run first**: filter Acquire/EF/Microns for the §3 profile, request read-only
  Stripe/bank on 2-3, build the model + tech review. If nothing clears the gates in ~2-3 months,
  that's signal the clean-deal price doesn't work for him — keep the capital.
